paragraphs.heading: Earth's companion
paragraphs.text: The Moon is Earth's only natural satellite. It travels an elliptical path whose distance from Earth changes through the year and averages about 378,000 kilometers. Measured against both Earth and the Sun, one lap, called a lunar month, takes 29.5 days.

paragraphs.heading: Locked in place
paragraphs.text: Earth and the Moon pull on each other, and the pull is strongest on the sides that face each other. These tidal forces are the main cause of Earth's tides, and they have also turned the Moon so the same near side always faces Earth. This tidal locking makes the Moon's day as long as its month. Because the Moon is seen from slightly different angles, an effect called libration, about 59% of its surface is visible from Earth.

paragraphs.heading: Size and makeup
paragraphs.text: Geophysicists class the Moon as a planetary-mass object. It has 1.2% of Earth's mass and is 3,474 km across, roughly a quarter of Earth's width. It is bigger than any known dwarf planet, the fifth-largest moon in the Solar System, and the largest compared with its own planet. On its surface, gravity pulls about one-sixth as hard as on Earth. Its body is differentiated and terrestrial, with only a tiny hydrosphere, atmosphere and magnetic field.

paragraphs.heading: Craters and dark seas
paragraphs.text: Regolith dust covers the surface, mostly fine material knocked off the crust by impacts. Impact craters mark the crust, and some younger ones have bright streaks that look like rays. Until 1.2 billion years ago, lava welled up, mostly on the thinner near side, and filled old craters. As it cooled, it formed the dark basalt plains, called maria ('seas'), that stand out today.

paragraphs.heading: Born from a collision
paragraphs.text: The Moon is thought to have formed from material thrown off Earth when a Mars-sized body struck it. Dating of crystals from its early magma ocean suggests it formed 4.35 billion years ago, late in the Solar System's history.

paragraphs.heading: In our sky
paragraphs.text: From a distance, the Moon's day and night show up as its phases, and when it passes through Earth's shadow a lunar eclipse can be seen. It looks about as big as the Sun in our sky, so during a total solar eclipse it covers the Sun completely. It is the brightest object in the night sky because it looks so large, even though its surface reflects light about as well as asphalt.

paragraphs.heading: Visiting the Moon
paragraphs.text: The first spacecraft to reach another world went to the Moon: the Soviet Luna 1 flew past in 1959, and Luna 2 struck it on purpose. In 1966 Luna 9 made the first soft landing and Luna 10 entered orbit. Apollo 8 carried people into lunar orbit on December 24, 1968, and Apollo 11 landed on July 20, 1969, making the Moon the only world beyond Earth that humans have visited. By 1972, six Apollo missions had landed twelve people. New robotic missions, especially to confirm water there, have led to plans to return, including the Artemis program and its crewed Artemis II flyby of 2026.

paragraphs.heading: Its names
paragraphs.text: English writes the name with a capital M, and the IAU does the same, keeping lowercase moons for the satellites of other planets. The word comes from Old English mōna, which traces back to a Proto-Indo-European word for month. The Latin name is lūna, the source of the English adjective lunar. The Greek word selḗnē lines up with the prefix seleno-, as in selenography, the study of the lunar surface.
